re-b1-listing-from-notes.q: Your rough notes for a listing never mention square footage, but a good MLS description usually includes it. What should Claude do?
options: Estimate a reasonable square footage based on typical units
Skip mentioning square footage anywhere in the output, silently
List it under "Missing facts to confirm" rather than guessing at it
Use the average square footage of nearby listings as a stand-in
re-b1-listing-from-notes.why: The guardrail prompt explicitly tells Claude to surface any normally-expected fact that's missing from your notes under a "Missing facts to confirm" list instead of guessing at it.

re-b1-listing-from-notes.q: The prompt states the "use only my notes" rule twice — once as a rule, once as an instruction to list missing facts. Why the repetition?
options: Repetition has no functional purpose here, just habit
Because Claude ignores any instruction stated only once
It's required for MLS compliance specifically
It reinforces the constraint so the model surfaces gaps instead of smoothing over missing information with a plausible-sounding guess
re-b1-listing-from-notes.why: Stating the constraint both as a rule and as an explicit fallback instruction is what stops the model from quietly filling a gap with a plausible detail instead of flagging it.

re-b1-listing-from-notes.q: You want to verify the guardrail against inventing facts is actually working. What's the right way to test it?
options: Testing with already-polished notes hides whether the invent-nothing guardrail is actually working — test it with genuinely rough, incomplete notes
That's the best way to test since it mirrors reality most closely
Polished notes always generate a materially better draft
The type of notes used for testing doesn't matter
re-b1-listing-from-notes.why: Polished, already-complete notes give the model nothing to fill in, so they can't reveal whether the anti-invention guardrail actually holds when facts are genuinely missing.

re-b2-improve-listing-description.q: You ask Claude to rewrite a listing, and "updated kitchen" comes back as "fully renovated kitchen." What happened?
options: Nothing went wrong — this is a normal stylistic improvement
The rewrite silently changed a fact — this is exactly the kind of risky wording the "Facts changed or added" self-audit is meant to catch
"Fully renovated" and "updated" always mean the same thing legally
This is fine as long as the target word count was met
re-b2-improve-listing-description.why: "Fully renovated" is a stronger, different claim than "updated," and the required self-audit step exists precisely to flag this kind of quiet fact drift before it's published.

re-b2-improve-listing-description.q: Under the rewrite prompt's rules, what is Claude allowed to change versus not change?
options: May add new features not in the original to make the copy more compelling
May not change word order or phrasing at all
May reorder, cut filler, and use more vivid wording for the same fact, but may not add any new fact, feature, or claim
May only shorten the text, never rephrase it
re-b2-improve-listing-description.why: The prompt explicitly permits reordering and tightening language while banning any new fact, feature, upgrade, or claim beyond what the original text already stated.

re-b2-improve-listing-description.q: You run the rewrite prompt without giving a target word count. What's the likely consequence?
options: Word count has no bearing on anything in this workflow
Skipping the word count always makes the rewrite shorter
MLS description fields have no length limits to worry about
The rewrite may come back a different length than what your MLS field actually allows
re-b2-improve-listing-description.why: Without a specified target length, the rewrite has no length constraint to match your MLS character limit against, risking a draft that doesn't fit the destination field.

re-b3-buyer-followup-emails.q: A buyer loved the balcony and asked about the HOA fee during a showing. What makes a follow-up email actually effective, per the lesson?
options: Referencing at least one specific detail from what the buyer liked or asked about during the showing
Sending a generic "just checking in!" template quickly
Adding several different calls to action to maximize the odds of a reply
Using urgency language like "won't last long" to prompt a fast reply
re-b3-buyer-followup-emails.why: Referencing a specific reaction from the buyer's own walkthrough is the single biggest lever for reply rates — generic emails read as mass mail and get ignored.

re-b3-buyer-followup-emails.q: Why does the prompt require ending with one clear next step instead of several different asks?
options: Multiple asks are always more effective at generating a response
A single, low-friction next step is easier for the buyer to respond to than juggling multiple asks
Email clients technically block messages containing more than one question
It's a spam-filter requirement, not a persuasion choice
re-b3-buyer-followup-emails.why: One clear, low-friction ask is easier to act on than several competing requests, which is why the prompt explicitly bans multiple asks in a single follow-up.

re-b3-buyer-followup-emails.q: An agent adds "this unit won't last long!" to a first follow-up email to create urgency. What's wrong with this?
options: Urgency language builds trust with hesitant buyers
Urgency language is a required real-estate marketing standard
Urgency or scarcity language on a first follow-up can feel pushy and risks losing a hesitant buyer's trust
This concern only applies to luxury listings
re-b3-buyer-followup-emails.why: The prompt explicitly bans pressure tactics like "won't last long" because urgency language on an early follow-up tends to read as pushy and can cost you a hesitant buyer's trust.

re-b4-seller-update-messages.q: This week's buyer feedback on a seller's listing was lukewarm — one buyer said the price felt high. What should the weekly update do?
options: Soften the feedback so the seller stays positive and motivated
Omit the feedback entirely since there's no offer yet
Wait to send an update until there's positive feedback to report
Report the feedback honestly, including negative comments, without softening or omitting it
re-b4-seller-update-messages.why: The prompt's core guardrail explicitly forbids softening or omitting negative feedback, since sellers lose trust fast when they later learn feedback was worse than what they were told.

re-b4-seller-update-messages.q: Multiple showings this week mention the same concern about parking. Why ask Claude to flag that repeated pattern?
options: A repeated pattern across multiple showings' feedback is an early warning signal for a pricing or staging conversation that needs to happen
Repetition should be removed from the update to keep it concise
Patterns in feedback are only useful for the buyer's agent, not the seller's
Feedback patterns rarely point to anything actionable
re-b4-seller-update-messages.why: A pattern repeating across independent showings is a much stronger signal than any single comment, and surfacing it turns a routine update into an early cue for a pricing or staging conversation.

re-b4-seller-update-messages.q: A draft update implies strong buyer interest even though the actual numbers were three showings and no offers. What's the problem?
options: A little optimism helps keep sellers motivated during a slow week
Letting the update imply more buyer interest than the actual numbers support undermines the trust-building purpose of an honest update
Sellers generally prefer inflated updates over accurate ones
This is only a problem if the seller later finds out independently
re-b4-seller-update-messages.why: The whole value of a weekly update is that sellers can trust it even when news is lukewarm; inflating perceived interest defeats that purpose regardless of whether it's ever discovered.

re-b5-summarize-property-documents-safel.q: An inspection report mentions a water stain but includes no repair cost estimate. Should the summary include a repair cost?
options: Yes, a reasonable market-based repair cost estimate is helpful
Only estimate costs for safety-related items, not cosmetic ones
No — do not predict a repair cost unless a specific cost is explicitly stated in the document
Yes, but only when the item appears in the "major issues" category
re-b5-summarize-property-documents-safel.why: The prompt explicitly bans predicting repair costs unless the document itself states one, since an invented cost is exactly the kind of plausible-sounding addition that creates liability.

re-b5-summarize-property-documents-safel.q: Why does the summary prompt require an exact disclaimer sentence at the end of every output?
options: It's purely a stylistic formality with no real function
It's required only for inspection reports, not seller disclosures
It replaces the need to attach the original document to the summary
It clearly labels the summary as a convenience tool, not a substitute for the full document or advice from a licensed professional
re-b5-summarize-property-documents-safel.why: The required disclaimer keeps every summary you forward clearly labeled as a convenience tool rather than the document of record, protecting both you and your client.

re-b5-summarize-property-documents-safel.q: You've generated a clean summary of a seller disclosure. How should you share it with your client?
options: The summary should be shared alongside the full original document, never in place of it
It's fine to forward the summary alone since it covers everything relevant
Attaching both the summary and original document tends to confuse clients
The original document becomes optional once a summary exists
re-b5-summarize-property-documents-safel.why: The workflow explicitly says to share the summary alongside the full original document, never instead of it, since the summary is a convenience layer, not a replacement.

re-b6-property-faq-from-listing.q: A buyer's likely FAQ question about property taxes wasn't included in your facts sheet. How should the FAQ answer it?
options: Estimate a reasonable tax figure based on the listing price
"Ask your agent for current details" instead of guessing at a figure that wasn't provided
Omit the tax question from the FAQ entirely, without explanation
Provide a national average property tax rate as a placeholder
re-b6-property-faq-from-listing.why: The prompt's explicit fallback instruction is to answer unknowns with "Ask your agent for current details" rather than let Claude guess at a figure like taxes or HOA fees.

re-b6-property-faq-from-listing.q: Why does the lesson cap each FAQ answer at 1-3 sentences?
options: Longer answers aren't technically supported by the output format
It's an MLS compliance requirement for FAQ documents
It keeps the sheet scannable and printable on a single page for buyers at an open house
Shorter answers are inherently more factually accurate
re-b6-property-faq-from-listing.why: Buyers won't read past a single page at an open house, so keeping each answer brief is what keeps the whole FAQ printable and scannable.

re-b6-property-faq-from-listing.q: A new question keeps coming up at recent showings that isn't in your existing FAQ sheet. What should you do?
options: FAQs should stay static once created, to maintain consistency
Recurring buyer questions rarely change over the life of a listing
Updating the FAQ requires rebuilding it from scratch each time
The FAQ should be updated whenever a new recurring question comes up at a showing
re-b6-property-faq-from-listing.why: The lesson's workflow explicitly includes updating the FAQ whenever a new recurring question emerges, keeping the sheet aligned with what buyers actually ask.

re-i1-neighborhood-guide-copy.q: A draft of neighborhood copy includes a specific walk score and a school rating you never supplied. What went wrong?
options: These are exactly the specific, checkable claims a model will confidently invent unless explicitly banned — a core guardrail failure here
This is normal, helpful enrichment of the neighborhood copy
Walk scores don't need verification since they're considered public data
This is fine as long as it's disclosed to the client afterward
re-i1-neighborhood-guide-copy.why: School ratings, walk scores, and safety claims are exactly the specific, checkable details a model will confidently invent for a recognizable neighborhood name unless the prompt explicitly bans them.

re-i1-neighborhood-guide-copy.q: Why does the lesson treat the fair-housing rule as a standing instruction applied to every sentence, not a one-time reminder?
options: Because fair-housing law technically only applies to headlines
Because fair-housing risk can appear in any sentence describing "who lives" somewhere, not just an obviously risky one
Because it's a formality without real practical risk
Because standing rules are just easier to write, not more effective
re-i1-neighborhood-guide-copy.why: Fair-housing risk can surface in any sentence that describes people rather than places, so the rule needs to apply continuously across the whole draft, not just to one obvious line.

re-i1-neighborhood-guide-copy.q: You want to state that a listing is a "12-minute drive to downtown." What should you check before using that claim?
options: Estimated times are fine as long as they're vaguely labeled as estimates
Drive and walk times don't need verification since they change constantly anyway
Only use drive/walk times you've personally measured or sourced — unverified specific claims are a credibility and accuracy risk
This concern only matters for luxury listings, not typical ones
re-i1-neighborhood-guide-copy.why: Specific, checkable claims like drive times are high-risk if unverified — the lesson requires using only times you've actually measured or can point to a source for.

re-i2-social-posts-new-listing.q: You take the same caption text and post it unchanged across Instagram, Facebook, and LinkedIn. What's the issue?
options: Nothing is wrong — consistency across platforms is ideal
LinkedIn and Instagram actually require identical formatting
Copy-pasting one caption everywhere helps prevent fair-housing issues
Each platform has different tone and format conventions — copy-pasting one caption everywhere ignores those platform-specific conventions
re-i2-social-posts-new-listing.why: A caption that works casually on Instagram reads wrong on LinkedIn's more professional, context-driven tone, which is why the lesson generates platform-specific versions from one brief.

re-i2-social-posts-new-listing.q: Why does the multi-platform prompt generate all four formats (IG, Facebook, LinkedIn, video script) from a single source brief?
options: It keeps the underlying facts identical across all four formats and avoids drift from re-explaining the listing each time
It's simply faster to write four completely separate briefs instead
Only one of the four generated formats is ever actually usable
It's required to avoid duplicate-content penalties on social platforms
re-i2-social-posts-new-listing.why: Generating from one grounded brief keeps facts consistent across every platform version, preventing the drift that comes from re-explaining the listing separately each time.

re-i2-social-posts-new-listing.q: A draft LinkedIn post describes the listing as "perfect for young professionals." What's the problem?
options: This is effective marketing language that boosts engagement with no downside
This creates fair-housing risk by describing the type of buyer or resident an area suits, rather than the property or location itself
This is fine as long as it doesn't explicitly reference race
This concern only applies in commercial real estate, not residential
re-i2-social-posts-new-listing.why: Steering language that describes who a listing suits, rather than what the property or location offers, is exactly the kind of fair-housing risk the prompt's guardrail is meant to prevent.

re-i3-objection-handling-scripts.q: An agent memorizes a Claude-generated negotiation script word-for-word before a tough conversation. What's the risk?
options: Memorized scripts work best since consistency wins negotiations
Memorizing word for word is required for professionalism in this context
A memorized script falls apart the instant the conversation goes off-path; talking points that are internalized adapt better
There's no real downside to memorizing a script verbatim
re-i3-objection-handling-scripts.why: The prompt asks for talking points rather than a rigid script precisely because a memorized script breaks down once the real conversation deviates, while internalized approaches can adapt.

re-i3-objection-handling-scripts.q: After generating response approaches, the prompt has Claude roleplay the other side pushing back. Why include this step?
options: It's an optional novelty feature with no real practical value
It only helps a seller's agent, not a buyer's agent
It replaces the need to actually know your own deal's facts
Roleplay practice is what turns this from a reading exercise into actual preparation for a live, unpredictable conversation
re-i3-objection-handling-scripts.why: Reading talking points silently is passive; roleplaying pushback is what actually builds the ability to respond under pressure in the real conversation.

re-i3-objection-handling-scripts.q: While preparing talking points, you let Claude supply a specific recent comp figure it wasn't given. What's the risk?
options: Only use your own verified comps and figures — the prompt explicitly bans invented numbers, using placeholders instead
Claude's estimated comps are reliable enough to cite directly in a live negotiation
Comp data doesn't really matter for objection handling
Any plausible-sounding number works fine since it's only for practice
re-i3-objection-handling-scripts.why: The prompt explicitly instructs Claude to use a placeholder instead of inventing a comp figure, since citing a made-up number in a live negotiation is a real credibility risk.

re-i4-local-market-research-perplexity.q: You ask Gemini Deep Research "how's the market?" with no area or timeframe specified. What's the likely result?
options: Gemini automatically narrows any query to the agent's exact ZIP code
Too broad a question fails to return locally specific data — you need to name the exact area and timeframe
This is actually the recommended way to start every market query
Vague questions tend to produce more accurate citations
re-i4-local-market-research-perplexity.why: Naming a specific area and timeframe is what gets Gemini Deep Research to run genuinely local queries; a vague question tends to return generic or national-level results instead.

re-i4-local-market-research-perplexity.q: Gemini Deep Research returns a cited market summary. Why click through 2-3 of the citations yourself instead of trusting the summary paragraph alone?
options: Deep Research summaries are usually fabricated and unreliable
It's required to unlock the client-ready summary feature
To confirm the underlying sources are actually recent and locally specific, not just present
Reports from Deep Research never actually contain citations
re-i4-local-market-research-perplexity.why: Having a citation doesn't guarantee it's current or genuinely local — opening a few links yourself is how you confirm the data actually supports the claim before using it with a client.

re-i4-local-market-research-perplexity.q: You have market research from a month ago and want to reuse it in a new client conversation. What should you do first?
options: Market data doesn't change meaningfully over a few weeks, so reuse is fine
Only re-run research if a client directly asks for a fresh source
Older research is actually more reliable since it's already been verified once
Market data ages fast — research should be re-run before reusing it in a new client conversation
re-i4-local-market-research-perplexity.why: The lesson notes that market data ages quickly, so research needs to be re-run before it's reused in a new conversation rather than treated as still current.

re-i5-lead-notes-weekly-activity-report.q: A lead never mentioned a buying timeline in your notes. What should the "suggested next action" column say for them?
options: A fact-finding action aimed at determining the lead's timeline, since the guardrail forbids assuming urgency that was never stated
Assume urgency and suggest pushing hard toward a quick close
Deprioritize the lead entirely since no timeline was given
Mark the lead as not interested and move on
re-i5-lead-notes-weekly-activity-report.why: The prompt explicitly instructs that when no timeline is stated, the suggested next action should be one that finds out the timeline, not one that assumes urgency that was never expressed.

re-i5-lead-notes-weekly-activity-report.q: Why does the lesson recommend keeping the same six-column lead table format every single week?
options: Identical formatting is a technical requirement of most CRM software
It's easier to scan and compare against last week's list when the format stays the same
Column headers are required to match specific MLS field names
It has no real benefit — it's just a stylistic convention
re-i5-lead-notes-weekly-activity-report.why: A consistent table structure week over week makes it easy to scan quickly and compare against the prior week's list, which is the point of a repeatable weekly process.

re-i5-lead-notes-weekly-activity-report.q: You're drafting the weekly activity report and consider rounding up a number to make the week look busier. What does the lesson say?
options: A little embellishment makes the weekly report look more impressive to a broker
Broker reports are informal enough that accuracy doesn't matter much
The report should state the numbers exactly as given, with no embellishment, since it needs to be a factual record the broker can trust
Padding is acceptable as long as the totals are roughly in the right range
re-i5-lead-notes-weekly-activity-report.why: The prompt requires reporting activity numbers exactly as given, with no embellishment, because the report's value depends on being a factual record the broker can rely on.

re-a1-property-landing-page-codex.q: Codex generates a working contact form for your new listing landing page. What should you do before deploying it?
options: Trust the visual preview and deploy immediately
Only check that the page loads and looks correct visually
Ask Codex to confirm it's safe, then deploy without reading the code yourself
Read the actual generated code — especially how the contact form handles submitted data — before accepting or deploying it
re-a1-property-landing-page-codex.why: The lesson's core guardrail is reviewing the diff and files, especially how submitted form data is handled, rather than trusting the preview or Codex's own assurance.

re-a1-property-landing-page-codex.q: Why does the landing-page prompt specify "static HTML/CSS/JS, no framework needed"?
options: It keeps the output reviewable and cheap to host without needing a build pipeline you'd have to maintain
Frameworks are generally broken when used with Codex
Static sites are specifically required by MLS rules
Static HTML/CSS/JS is the only format Codex is capable of producing
re-a1-property-landing-page-codex.why: Requesting plain static files keeps the site something you can actually read, host cheaply, and maintain without adopting a build pipeline for a single listing page.

re-a1-property-landing-page-codex.q: Before putting a new listing page live, what specific risk should you check for around the contact form?
options: Placeholder contact info is automatically stripped out at deploy time
Deploying with placeholder or sample contact info accidentally left in the page is a real risk worth explicitly checking for
This can't happen, since Codex validates all content before deployment
Placeholder text in a contact form is invisible to site visitors regardless
re-a1-property-landing-page-codex.why: The lesson explicitly flags deploying with leftover placeholder or sample contact information as a common mistake worth checking for before the page goes live.
